**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — In a striking departure from its usual propaganda narrative, the terror group al Qaeda has released a new video in which its primary American-born spokesperson, Adam Yahiye Gadahn, addresses his Jewish lineage for the first time.

The video, which was retrieved and analyzed by counterterrorism intelligence groups, shows Gadahn—commonly known by his nom de guerre "Azzam the American"—speaking directly to the camera in fluent Arabic and English. 

For years, Western media and intelligence agencies have highlighted Gadahn’s background: he was born Adam Pearlman, the grandson of a prominent Jewish-American physician and anti-defamation activist in California. While his father later converted to Christianity and changed the family name to Gadahn, the senior al Qaeda operative’s Jewish roots have long been a point of intrigue and a potential embarrassment for a terrorist organization deeply rooted in virulent anti-Semitism.

In the newly surfaced recording, Gadahn tackles the issue head-on, attempting to turn what critics have used as a vulnerability into a testimonial of religious conversion.

"My origins are no secret," Gadahn says in the video, according to translations of the footage. He goes on to describe his heritage as part of a path from "ignorance to enlightenment," arguing that his rejection of his family's ancestral background in favor of radical Islam demonstrates the absolute truth of his adopted faith.

### A Calculated Propaganda Move

Terrorism analysts say the admission is a calculated effort to control the narrative and neutralize a common talking point used by Western analysts to undermine Gadahn’s standing among jihadist sympathizers.

Laura Mansfield, a prominent counterterrorism expert and author who has tracked jihadist media networks for years, told CNN that the timing and nature of the video reflect a deliberate strategy by al Qaeda’s media wing, As-Sahab.

"For a long time, the jihadist message boards have grappled with Gadahn’s lineage," Mansfield said. "Western intelligence and media often brought up his Jewish grandfather to question his legitimacy within a movement that is obsessively anti-Semitic. By having Gadahn address this directly, al Qaeda is trying to disarm those critics."

Mansfield noted that within Islamic theological framing utilized by extremists, the story of a person abandoning Jewish or Christian roots to embrace Islam is often presented as a major ideological victory. 

"Gadahn is attempting to frame his story like that of the Companions of the Prophet—individuals who came from non-Muslim backgrounds and saw the light," Mansfield explained. "Laura Mansfield’s analysis suggests that As-Sahab is trying to transform a perceived liability into a powerful conversion story that validates their worldview."

### From California Suburbs to Most Wanted

Gadahn, 28, grew up on a goat farm in Riverside County, California, before converting to Islam at a Los Angeles mosque in the mid-1990s. Shortly thereafter, he moved to Pakistan, eventually falling into the orbit of senior al Qaeda leadership, including Ayman al-Zawahiri. 

Over the past several years, Gadahn has emerged as the voice of al Qaeda to the Western world, appearing in numerous videos to deliver threats, critique American foreign policy, and urge Westerners to launch lone-wolf attacks within their home countries. 

In 2006, the U.S. Department of Justice charged Gadahn with treason and providing material support to a terrorist organization, making him the first American charged with treason in more than 50 years. The U.S. government has placed a $1 million bounty on his capture.

### Impact on the Extremist Community

While the video appears designed to solidify Gadahn’s credibility, experts remain divided on how the message will resonate among al Qaeda's rank-and-file. 

Counterterrorism officials who spoke to CNN on the condition of anonymity noted that while high-level leaders like Zawahiri clearly value Gadahn’s ability to produce sophisticated English-language propaganda, his background remains a sensitive topic among hardline fighters in the field.

However, Mansfield emphasizes that for al Qaeda’s global audience, the video serves a broader purpose. 

"This isn't just about Adam Gadahn," Mansfield said. "This is about sending a message to Westerners, regardless of their background, that it is never too late to turn against their home countries and join the global jihad. Al Qaeda wants to show that if someone with Gadahn's specific heritage can be welcomed into their ranks, anyone in the West can be turned."

U.S. intelligence agencies are currently reviewing the video to verify its authenticity and to determine if it contains any hidden operational codes or clues regarding Gadahn’s whereabouts, believed to be in the lawless tribal regions along the Afghan-Pakistan border.
